catalog_citation: Cahill, Michael C. 1999. Aspects of the Morphology and Phonology of Kɔnni. PhD dissertation, The Ohio State University. xvi+541 pp. Open-access copy: OhioLINK ETD accession osu1488190595942418. Published as Cahill 2007, SIL International and UT Arlington Publications in Linguistics 141 (same chapter structure, sec. 6.7 'A note on stress'; not opened).
catalog_locator: Sec. 6.7 'A note on stress', pp. 465-466; chapter overview p. 39; tone inventory sec. 6.1.1 p. 338.
catalog_quote: In this phonology, I have not mentioned stress as a relevant quality of words. Most Gur phonological write-ups also do not discuss stress. ... In Konni, there do not seem to be any phonetic correlates of stress (vowel length, amplitude) which are significant and independent of tone. To illustrate, CECIL graphs for waveform, pitch, and amplitude of kùlí 'tortoise' and kùléhé 'the tortoises' are shown below. ... Note above that while the first two syllables in both words (spoken in isolation in the same recording session) are LH, in (A) the second syllable has greater amplitude, while in (B) the first syllable has greater amplitude. If "articulatory energy" is what the other Gur writers are referring to when they speak of "stress", then this does not seem to be consistent in Konni. Though more research undoubtedly needs to be done in this area, it appears that stress is not phonologically contrastive or distinctive in Konni. (pp. 465-466) -- Chapter overview, p. 39: Since some African languages have been analyzed as having stress, the question is examined for Konni, with the conclusion that stress plays no part in the phonology of Konni. -- Sec. 6.1.1, p. 338: Konni has two basic tone levels, High and Low. A downstepped High tone also may occur after a High.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog has no record for konn1242 and no existing statements; this is the first explicit stress statement found for the language. The open_url was the the Harvard library catalogue discovery record, which points to OhioLINK ETD osu1488190595942418; the PDF was downloaded directly from the OhioLINK ETD send_file endpoint (open access, 17.1 MB, ABBYY text, 560 PDF pages).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kɔnni has two basic tone levels, High and Low, plus a downstepped High (p. 338). Cahill looks for stress explicitly and finds no phonetic correlate (vowel length, amplitude) that is significant and independent of tone; amplitude peaks fall on different syllables in the two measured words (kùlî 'tortoise' vs kùléhé 'the tortoises'); his conclusion is that stress is not phonologically contrastive or distinctive and plays no part in the phonology. No stress position is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Author hedges: 'more research undoubtedly needs to be done in this area'. He notes that other Gur descriptions (Dagaare: Antilla & Bodomo 1996; Supyire: Carlson 1994; Buli: Kroger 1992) speak of stress on penultimate or root-initial syllables or of greater 'articulatory energy' on initial syllables, and suggests word-initial position rather than stress may be the relevant property there.
new_statements.identity_note: Cahill 1999 describes Kɔnni of Yikpabongo, Northern Region, Ghana (the only variety in the literature); no dialect split is at issue. Works 4 and 5 (Berwick & Chomsky 2019; Rezac 2004) are not about Kɔnni at all and appear to be Glottolog misattributions; works 6 and 7 are cross-linguistic SIL working papers.

new_statements.relation_note: Same passage as the catalog record (world-r3, Cahill 1999 sec. 6.7) and as the verified existing statement; the catalog classification tonal stands. Wording nuance only: the source does make an explicit statement about stress (none contrastive, no tone-independent correlates), so 'tonal; explicit statement: no contrastive word stress' is more exact than the label 'no stress statement'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kɔnni is a tone language (High, Low, downstepped High); the author states that stress plays no role in its phonology: no phonetic correlate of stress (length, amplitude) is significant and independent of tone, amplitude prominence falls inconsistently on the first or second syllable, and stress is not contrastive or distinctive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none (no word stress recognised at all).
new_statements.exceptions: None as exceptions; the author illustrates that in kùléhé 'the tortoises' the second syllable has greater amplitude while in kùlî 'tortoise' the first does, i.e. 'articulatory energy' is not consistent, and adds that more research is needed. He reviews Gur claims (Dagaare penultimate stress per Antilla & Bodomo; Supyire and Buli initial-syllable 'stress'/'articulatory energy') and suggests these may be word-initial position effects rather than stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All works describe Kɔnni [kma] of the Koma area (Yikpabongo and neighbouring villages), Northern Region, Ghana; Cahill's dissertation data are mainly the Yikpabongo dialect (Nangurima dialect noted as differing, e.g. /h/); the 2015 handout's speakers (Naaza Solomon Dintigi, Mumuni Salifu Barnabas) were recorded in Tamale; the handout misprints the ISO code as [kom], the published chapter gives [kma].

new_statements.quote: In Kɔnni, there are no words with all Low tones; a High must occur somewhere in the word. Some words have no underlying High; if not, one will be inserted. [...] Beyond that, there may also be a connection between High tone and prominence in general. One phonetic correlate of stress is higher pitch, and it may be that, for lexical items in many languages, there must be some prominent syllable. For tone languages, that prominence manifests itself as the (marked) High tone.

tone_statements.quote: Kɔnni ([kma], Gur family) has two underlying tones, High (H) and Low (L). These may combine as rising (LH) and falling (HL) contours on single syllables. A second High may be downstepped from the preceding High (HꜝH). This sequence can appear on adjacent syllables or on a single syllable as a second type of falling tone. The tone-bearing unit is the syllable, to which one or two autosegmental tones may associate. A detailed presentation and analysis of Kɔnni tone can be found in Cahill (2007).
tone_statements.summary: 2 level tones H, L; LH/HL contours on one syllable; downstepped H; polar questions add L/LH/HLH tonal autosegments (floating=yes); fn. 4 downdrift. H'.

tone_statements.citation: Cahill, Michael. 2004. Tone Polarity in Kɔnni Nouns. Studies in African Linguistics 33(1): 1-33. doi:10.32473/sal.v33i1.107337
tone_statements.quote: Kɔnni's level tones are transcribed as High, Low, and downstepped High. These can combined to form one rising tone (Low to High) and two falling tones (High to Low, and High to downstepped High). The H!H contour on a single TBU reported here is rare in the literature. [...] a. The syllable is the tone-bearing unit. [...] b. There is no HLH sequence phonetically within a word. When one would be created by concatenation of morphemes, the second H spreads, resulting in H!HH surface pattern [...] c. Contour tones are only found on the final syllable of a word [...] e. Underlying High tones do not remain floating, but Low tones can float between Highs, causing downstep.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 2-4, sec. 1.1 and generalisations (4a-e); polar NC1 plural suffix pp. 4-5, 28-29
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Kɔnni has three level tones (High, Low, downstepped High) and three contours (LH, HL, H!H), with the syllable as tone-bearing unit, contours restricted to word-final syllables, a ban on HLH inside a word, and downstep caused by a floating Low. The Noun Class 1 plural suffix carries a polar tone (opposite to the preceding stem tone), which the paper analyses with a morpheme-specific POLAR constrain

tone_statements.citation: Cahill, Michael (2000). Noun Classes and Phonology in Konni. Journal of West African Languages 28. pp. 49-69.
tone_statements.quote: As in most nominal suffixes, the suffixes of noun class 1 are H-toned, with the notable exception of the plural morpheme /-A/, which is either H- or L-toned, having the opposite tone of the preceding tone. This tonal polarity is discussed in §2.2. [p. 52] ... This noun class contains the only forms I am aware of which have a contour tone on a non-final syllable, found always in the plural forms such as 'friends, fathers'. They are always followed by a downstepped H in the next syllable. [p. 55] ... If the root has a H lexical tone, the OCP, acting as a specific constraint, ensures that the inserted tone is not identical to the root tone but is opposite, giving surface HL. ... the L tone is clearly the default in Konni (see Cahill 1999 for discussion) [p. 65]
tone_statements.check: quotation from the author's open copy, read 2026-09-25; not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: Two-tone (H/L) lexical-tone system with downstep; stems carry lexical H or L, nominal suffixes are H-toned except the class-1 plural suffix -a/-e, which shows tonal polarity (opposite to the last stem tone), analysed as a toneless suffix with default L insertion plus an OCP constraint; -sI plural surfaces with L in some downstep nouns (historical relic); contour tone on a non-final syllable only i

sources.quote: In this phonology, I have not mentioned stress as a relevant quality of words. Most Gur phonological write-ups also do not discuss stress. [...] In Konni, there do not seem to be any phonetic correlates of stress (vowel length, amplitude) which are significant and independent of tone. [...] Note above that while the first two syllables in both words (spoken in isolation in the same recording session) are LH, in (A) the second syllable has greater amplitude, while in (B) the first syllable has greater amplitude. If "articulatory energy" is what the other Gur writers are referring to when they speak of "stress", then this does not seem to be consistent in Konni. Though more research undoubtedly needs to be done in this area, it appears that stress is not phonologically contrastive or distinctive in Konni. (pp. 465-466) — p. 39: 'Since some African languages have been analyzed as having stress, the question is examined for Konni, with the conclusion that stress plays no part in the phonology of Konni.'

sources.quote: Kɔnni's level tones are transcribed as High, Low, and downstepped High. These can combined to form one rising tone (Low to High) and two falling tones (High to Low, and High to downstepped High). The H!H contour on a single TBU reported here is rare in the literature. [...] a. The syllable is the tone-bearing unit. [...] b. There is no HLH sequence phonetically within a word. When one would be created by concatenation of morphemes, the second H spreads, resulting in H!HH surface pattern [...] c. Contour tones are only found on the final syllable of a word [...] e. Underlying High tones do not remain floating, but Low tones can float between Highs, causing downstep.

sources.quote: As in most nominal suffixes, the suffixes of noun class 1 are H-toned, with the notable exception of the plural morpheme /-A/, which is either H- or L-toned, having the opposite tone of the preceding tone. This tonal polarity is discussed in §2.2. [p. 52] ... This noun class contains the only forms I am aware of which have a contour tone on a non-final syllable, found always in the plural forms such as 'friends, fathers'. They are always followed by a downstepped H in the next syllable. [p. 55] ... If the root has a H lexical tone, the OCP, acting as a specific constraint, ensures that the inserted tone is not identical to the root tone but is opposite, giving surface HL. ... the L tone is clearly the default in Konni (see Cahill 1999 for discussion) [p. 65]
sources.note: Two-tone (H/L) lexical-tone system with downstep; stems carry lexical H or L, nominal suffixes are H-toned except the class-1 plural suffix -a/-e, which shows tonal polarity (opposite to the last stem tone), analysed as a toneless suffix with default L insertion plus an OCP constraint; -sI plural surfaces with L in some downstep nouns (historical relic); contour tone on a non-final syllable only in class-5 plurals ('friends, fathers'), always followed by downstepped H; first- and second-person possessive pronouns are H-toned only with 'father'/'mother'. sources.quote: Kɔnni ([kma], Gur family) has two underlying tones, High (H) and Low (L). These may combine as rising (LH) and falling (HL) contours on single syllables. A second High may be downstepped from the preceding High (HꜝH). This sequence can appear on adjacent syllables or on a single syllable as a second type of falling tone. The tone-bearing unit is the syllable, to which one or two autosegmental tones may associate. A detailed presentation and analysis of Kɔnni tone can be found in Cahill (2007).
sources.note: 2 level tones H, L; LH/HL contours on one syllable; downstepped H; polar questions add L/LH/HLH tonal autosegments (floating=yes); fn. 4 downdrift. H'.

sources.quote: In Kɔnni, a Gur language of northern Ghana, a segmentless High tone is the morpheme which marks the associative construction in third person, as in 'his stone' or 'child's stick'. The evidence for this is that the head noun of every such construction for third person as possessor has a High tone on its initial syllable. It is only the third person, singular or plural, that has the High tone as associative marker

sources.note: Confirms the catalog's tonal kind (High and Low tones on citation-form nouns; the diacritic key on p. 34 lists Low, High, Falling, Rising, Mid, Downstep for the survey generally). Adds detail not in the entry: a purely tonal (floating High) associative morpheme in 3rd-person possessive constructions, an H!H downstep contour on a single syllable (u zá!sìŋ 'his fish', u dá!aŋ 'his stick'), and leftward spread of High from a suffix (tíígé, tíígéhé), cited as a counterexample to the 'tones always spread right' claim. Footnote 25 (p. 58): *(H) is undominated in Kɔnni and some spreading is leftward.

sources.quote: Kɔnni has three phonological surface tones: High (á), Low (à), and downstepped High (!á). These can combine to form one rising tone (low to high) and two falling tones (high to low and high to downstepped high).
